name: Impairment of Unique Digital Assets
title: Impairment of Unique Digital Assets
answer: Impairment of unique digital assets covers non-fungible tokens, tokenized collectibles, digital art, virtual land, in-game items, and other distinct on-chain assets that are not interchangeable. It sits within digital asset accounting, where the central question is whether the carrying amount on the balance sheet still reflects the value the entity can recover. The scope includes assets held for use, held for sale, or held as inventory, because the accounting model changes with intent and with the nature of the asset. It also covers the related disclosures that explain how impairment losses were measured and why they occurred.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Impairment of unique digital assets covers non-fungible tokens, tokenized collectibles, digital art, virtual land, in-game items, and other distinct on-chain assets that are not interchangeable. It sits within digital asset accounting, where the central question is whether the carrying amount on the balance sheet still reflects the value the entity can recover. The scope includes assets held for use, held for sale, or held as inventory, because the accounting model changes with intent and with the nature of the asset. It also covers the related disclosures that explain how impairment losses were measured and why they occurred.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the entity's ledger and subledger, wallet and custody records, and the blockchain data that proves ownership and transfer history. Valuation inputs come from marketplace sales, auction results, floor prices for comparable collections, and any appraisals or internal models used when no active market exists. Accounting systems, ERP modules, and digital asset tracking tools hold the carrying amounts, cost basis, and impairment test dates. Because unique assets trade infrequently, the infrastructure must also capture off-chain evidence such as bids, listings, and provenance documents.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The accountant identifies the asset, confirms its cost or revalued carrying amount, and tests for impairment when events or changes in circumstances indicate the value may have fallen. For indefinite-lived intangibles, the test is typically annual and whenever indicators appear, while finite-lived assets are tested when triggered. The recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use, and an impairment loss is recognized when carrying amount exceeds that amount. For unique assets, valuation often relies on level 3 inputs, comparable sales, and discounted cash flow or market approaches, with documentation of the key assumptions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance covers who may hold, transfer, or pledge the asset, and what rights the token actually conveys, because a token may represent ownership of a digital file, a license, or only a record on a blockchain. Provenance matters for impairment because chain of custody, authenticity, and legal enforceability affect recoverable amount and the risk of fraud or duplicate claims. Controls should separate custody from accounting, require dual approval for transfers, and keep evidence of valuation inputs and impairment decisions. Disclosure obligations and audit readiness depend on the applicable framework, whether IFRS, US GAAP, or local rules, and on the entity's own policies for digital assets.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Practice is moving toward more consistent valuation guidance for unique digital assets, with greater use of observable market data and standardized impairment indicators. Regulators and standard setters continue to examine how crypto assets, including non-fungible tokens, should be measured and disclosed, which may reduce the range of acceptable treatments over time. Automation and on-chain analytics are likely to make impairment testing more frequent and more data driven, while audit firms will expect stronger evidence for level 3 assumptions. The direction is toward clearer rules for provenance, custody, and recoverable amount, even as the assets themselves remain illiquid and hard to compare.
